Module 8 · 170–210 minutes

Decoding and thresholds

Assumes: Independent error probabilities, majority decoding, and suppression ratios from Module 1 · Stabilizer equivalence, CSS check matrices, and logical classes from Module 2 · Primal and dual strings and winding from Module 3, and the canonical rotated patch from Module 4 · Detection events, detector error models, and circuit noise from Module 7

Requires: Measuring a surface code: circuits, detectors and Google's memory experiments · Enables: Independent application

By the end, you can
  • Derive a sufficient low-noise condition by counting dangerous residual loops.
  • Compute conditional logical-class probabilities and translate their sums into Ising partition functions.
  • Decide whether an erased set supports a logical operator and apply a leaf-peeling correction on a tree.
  • Construct log-odds edge weights, find a small matching, and identify information that matching discards.
  • Separate decoder latency from throughput and identify when pending syndrome data prevents feed-forward.
  • Convert an explicit suppression model into a minimum odd distance and an honest qubit count.
  1. 8.1 · Counting error chains: why a threshold exists
  2. 8.2 · The statistical-mechanics mapping
  3. 8.3 · Erasures and percolation
  4. 8.4 · Matching decoders
  5. 8.5 · Degeneracy and maximum likelihood
  6. 8.6 · Correlation-aware and learned decoders
  7. 8.7 · Real-time decoding
  8. 8.8 · From suppression to overhead
  9. 8.9 · Reconstruct and transfer

Protection depends on what the record contains, how the decoder uses it, and whether the answer arrives in time. We will follow those questions from one error loop to a qubit budget. A natural break comes after erasures.

Take the same stored-qubit experiment and change only the program that interprets its measurement record. In a reanalysis of Google's Sycamore data, ordinary matching gives more logical errors for the larger code. A tensor-network decoder gives fewer. The hardware record has not changed. What did the second program see that the first missed?

These are opposite finite-distance trends Learning to Decode the Surface Code with a Recurrent, Transformer-Based Neural Network, PDF pp. 7–8 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08148-8. Google's original analysis used belief matching and tensor-network decoding, both of which improved with distance Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit, PDF p. 5 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-022-05434-1. Two code sizes alone do not locate an asymptotic threshold. To understand the comparison, we need to ask what each decoder optimizes.

Physical probabilities are per data-qubit use in the code-capacity examples and per stated fault location in circuit models; experimental logical rates are per QEC cycle.

§

8.1 · Counting error chains: why a threshold exists

A long error loop has many possible shapes. Each shape also requires many faults. A safe noise regime exists when the probability cost beats the growing number of shapes.

Use an L×LL\times LL×L toric code with distance d=Ld=Ld=L. Each edge independently suffers a ZZZ error with probability ppp; checks are perfect. The decoder returns a chain RRR with the observed syndrome and the fewest possible edges. Write EEE for the actual error. Their residual C=E⊕RC=E\oplus RC=E⊕R has no endpoints. As in Module 3, recovery fails if this closed set winds around the torus. The symbol ⊕\oplus⊕ means addition modulo two: an edge present twice cancels.

A nontrivial residual contains a simple nontrivial cycle γ\gammaγ. Let ℓ\ellℓ be its length and ∣E∩γ∣|E\cap\gamma|∣E∩γ∣ the number of its edges that were faulty. Minimum-weight recovery imposes

ℓ≥d,∣E∩γ∣≥ℓ/2.\ell\geq d,\qquad |E\cap\gamma|\geq\ell/2.ℓ≥d,∣E∩γ∣≥ℓ/2.
(8.1)
Derivation · Compare the recovery with its loop toggle

Toggle every edge of γ\gammaγ in the recovery. Since a cycle has zero boundary, R′=R⊕γR'=R\oplus\gammaR′=R⊕γ has the same syndrome. Minimality of RRR requires

0≤∣R′∣−∣R∣=ℓ−2∣R∩γ∣.0\leq |R'|-|R|=\ell-2|R\cap\gamma|.0≤∣R′∣−∣R∣=ℓ−2∣R∩γ∣.

Every edge of γ⊆E⊕R\gamma\subseteq E\oplus Rγ⊆E⊕R belongs to exactly one of E,RE,RE,R. Thus ∣E∩γ∣=ℓ−∣R∩γ∣≥ℓ/2|E\cap\gamma|=\ell-|R\cap\gamma|\geq\ell/2∣E∩γ∣=ℓ−∣R∩γ∣≥ℓ/2. A nontrivial cycle has at least ddd edges by the code's distance. If the residual has branches, decompose its even-degree graph into simple cycles; a nonzero winding parity requires a nontrivial member of that decomposition. Failure therefore supplies a long cycle with at least half its edges faulty.

How many faults must the loop contain?

For a nontrivial residual cycle under this minimum-weight decoder, which condition is necessary?

At least half must be faulty. Otherwise the recovery occupies more than half, and toggling the loop would shorten it without changing its syndrome. The decoder itself can supply the rest of the failing loop.

Your prediction

For one specified ℓ\ellℓ-edge cycle, independence makes its fault count binomial. Call it dangerous when at least half its edges are faulty. For 0≤p≤1/20\leq p\leq1/20≤p≤1/2,

Pr⁡(γ dangerous)=∑j=⌈ℓ/2⌉ℓ(ℓj)pj(1−p)ℓ−j≤[2p(1−p)]ℓ.\Pr(\gamma\text{ dangerous}) =\sum_{j=\lceil\ell/2\rceil}^{\ell}\binom\ell j p^j(1-p)^{\ell-j} \leq[2\sqrt{p(1-p)}]^\ell.Pr(γ dangerous)=j=⌈ℓ/2⌉∑ℓ​(jℓ​)pj(1−p)ℓ−j≤[2p(1−p)​]ℓ.

pj(1−p)ℓ−j=[p(1−p)]ℓ/2(p1−p)j−ℓ/2≤[p(1−p)]ℓ/2.p^j(1-p)^{\ell-j}=[p(1-p)]^{\ell/2} \left(\frac p{1-p}\right)^{j-\ell/2}\leq[p(1-p)]^{\ell/2}.pj(1−p)ℓ−j=[p(1−p)]ℓ/2(1−pp​)j−ℓ/2≤[p(1−p)]ℓ/2.

The remaining binomial coefficients sum to at most 2ℓ2^\ell2ℓ. Multiplication gives the stated bound; p=0p=0p=0 follows directly. This is a bound on a necessary event for failure, not the probability that every edge is faulty. That latter probability is pℓp^\ellpℓ and would miss the recovery edges.

There are L2L^2L2 choices of starting vertex. Counting all nonbacktracking walks also counts open paths and counts each loop many times. A union bound can tolerate this excess: the probability of any dangerous loop is no greater than the sum of their bounds. With r=6p(1−p)<1r=6\sqrt{p(1-p)}<1r=6p(1−p)​<1,

Pfail≤4L23∑ℓ=d∞rℓ=4L23rd1−r.P_{\rm fail}\leq\frac{4L^2}{3}\sum_{\ell=d}^{\infty}r^\ell =\frac{4L^2}{3}\frac{r^d}{1-r}.Pfail​≤34L2​ℓ=d∑∞​rℓ=34L2​1−rrd​.

A sufficient noise region

The elementary count converges when 36p(1−p)<136p(1-p)<136p(1−p)<1. On p<1/2p<1/2p<1/2, its smaller quadratic root gives

p<1−8/92=0.02859548….p<\frac{1-\sqrt{8/9}}2=0.02859548\ldots.p<21−8/9​​=0.02859548….

A sharper walk count uses the square-lattice connective constant, the exponential growth rate of self-avoiding paths. Dennis et al. quote μ≈2.638\mu\approx2.638μ≈2.638 Topological quantum memory, PDF p. 20 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1063/1.1499754. Replacing the branching factor by this asymptotic growth rate gives 2μp(1−p)<12\mu\sqrt{p(1-p)}<12μp(1−p)​<1, or p<0.03731704…p<0.03731704\ldotsp<0.03731704…, conventionally quoted as 0.03730.03730.0373. The refined argument retains polynomial counting factors. Neither root identifies the actual critical noise: both counts include many paths that cannot cause the same failure.

What has the bound established?

What does the convergent path sum prove for the stated toric-code model?

Your answer

You can now prove that this decoder has a nonzero safe noise regime. To find the best possible decision, we must add the probabilities of errors that act alike.

8.2 · The statistical-mechanics mapping

Two errors can leave the same flags and have the same effect on the logical qubits. Their probabilities belong in the same pile. The decoder should compare the piles.

Start with the open repetition chain, where the ambiguity is small enough to see without a sum over many patterns.

Take d=5,w=1,p=0.1d=5,w=1,p=0.1d=5,w=1,p=0.1. The odds are 95−2=7299^{5-2}=72995−2=729, so the posterior of the weight-one pattern is 729/(729+1)=729/730≈0.998630729/(729+1)=729/730\approx0.998630729/(729+1)=729/730≈0.998630. A rare complementary pattern is still possible.

A higher free energy means a smaller posterior. Inserting a winding loop changes the sector, equivalently a twisted boundary condition. It creates a logical domain-wall cost; flipping one local face does not. The ordered phase resists this system-spanning change in alignment. On its Nishimori line the typical cost grows with lattice size, suppressing competing sectors Topological quantum memory, PDF p. 16 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1063/1.1499754.

Minimum-weight inference chooses a lowest-energy chain. Class inference chooses the lowest free energy, including the multiplicity of competing chains. A winding insertion twists the boundary condition. In the ordered phase, the system resists that global change in alignment, and its typical free-energy cost grows with size Topological quantum memory, PDF p. 16 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1063/1.1499754.

What does the optimal decision compare?

How does a decoder use stabilizer-equivalent errors optimally under the specified prior?

Your answer

What changes when check reports can be wrong?

For a surface code with repeated noisy checks, which statistical model represents the histories?

Time supplies the extra direction. Wrong reports occupy time-like links in the error-history graph. Summing equivalent histories leads to a random-plaquette gauge model, rather than the two-dimensional spin model of one perfect syndrome.

Your prediction

With independent data and report error probabilities both equal to ppp per round, Dennis et al. prove the sufficient bound p<0.0114p<0.0114p<0.0114 Topological quantum memory, PDF p. 20 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1063/1.1499754. Matching simulations estimate a threshold 0.0293±0.00020.0293\pm0.00020.0293±0.0002 for that phenomenological toric-code model Confinement-Higgs transition in a disordered gauge theory and the accuracy threshold for quantum memory, PDF p. 1 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1016/S0003-4916(02)00019-2. Neither number is a circuit-level gate threshold.

Tangent: the extra time direction

Optional. Repeated checks turn candidate error chains into histories. Local changes of a history sweep out surfaces; the auxiliary variables live on links, and a plaquette's weight depends on their product. This is the reason for the gauge-model name. For equal independent data and report noise, the optimal-class estimate is about 0.0330.0330.033, consistent with Ohno et al., as summarized in Stability of topologically-protected quantum computing proposals as seen through spin glasses, PDF pp. 14–15 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1088/1742-6596/473/1/012019. It is distinct from the matching value and the proven bound. Return to erasures.

You can now read a decoding threshold as a competition between logical-class probabilities. Next, we change the information available to the decoder by revealing the faulty locations.

§

8.3 · Erasures and percolation

Knowing which qubits were damaged removes most of the search. Recovery is guaranteed unless the marked set itself can hide a logical operator.

Let EEE now denote the known erasure set. Replace each lost qubit by I/2I/2I/2, which is equivalent to applying a uniformly random I,X,Y,ZI,X,Y,ZI,X,Y,Z at that position. No errors occur outside EEE, and syndrome extraction is ideal. We ask whether recovery works for every encoded state, not whether it can guess one particular hidden Pauli correctly.

Write SSS for the stabilizer group and N(S)N(S)N(S) for Paulis that commute with every stabilizer, ignoring overall phases. The known-support criterion is

E correctable⟺∄P∈N(S)∖S: supp⁡(P)⊆E.E\text{ correctable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \nexists P\in N(S)\setminus S:\ \operatorname{supp}(P)\subseteq E.E correctable⟺∄P∈N(S)∖S: supp(P)⊆E.
(8.10)
Derivation · Test which indistinguishable errors fit inside the erasure

Compare two possible errors P,QP,QP,Q supported inside EEE. Equal syndromes imply that P†QP^\dagger QP†Q commutes with all checks. If no logical Pauli fits inside EEE, this product must be a stabilizer. Correcting either possibility therefore corrects the other. If a nontrivial logical LLL does fit, III and LLL are both allowed errors with zero syndrome and different logical actions. No syndrome-based recovery can undo both on every encoded state. This is the stabilizer specialization of the known-support recovery condition Linear-Time Maximum Likelihood Decoding of Surface Codes over the Quantum Erasure Channel, PDF p. 2 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.2.033042. The criterion concerns the erased support, before any particular Pauli on it is revealed.

The primal graph carries ZZZ strings; the dual graph carries XXX strings. A seam is only where a periodic drawing was cut open. A path can cross it and still have two endpoints. A plaquette cycle has no endpoints but is a stabilizer. A winding cycle has no endpoints and a nontrivial logical action. These are three different geometric statements.

Does every erased cycle lose a logical qubit?

Which criterion decides recoverability?

A face boundary is a harmless stabilizer support. A winding cycle hides a logical operation. Equal-sized erased sets can therefore have different answers, and a single seam-crossing edge is still a tree.

How counts compete with weights
A separate count plot appears in every mode, showing rooted walks and the nonbacktracking bound from length 1 through the selected w. Counting mode also shows log10 of the counts, all-faulty weight and dangerous-loop weight through length 10. These auxiliary counts and weights are not measured failure probabilities. Horizontal: walk length w (dimensionless). Vertical: counts; log10 counts and weights in the comparison plot (dimensionless).

Method: Index all horizontal edges in row order, then all vertical edges. Track two seam-parity bits in separate primal and dual union-find forests. A closed cycle with nonzero parity identifies hidden logical support. For each trial, xorshift32 starts from seed + 65537L and draws one uniform number for every physical edge before testing any edges. Sort arrivals by that number, breaking ties by edge index. Insert edges until either graph closes a nontrivial cycle; its arrival is the critical probability. An erased set is uncorrectable when that critical value is strictly below p_e. Reuse these thresholds for every plotted probability and for the selected readout. Sampling proceeds in batches of at most eight trials between animation frames. The shape view reconstructs a witness through its spanning tree. Counting evaluates the rooted-walk table, c_w p^w and c_w [2 sqrt(p(1-p))]^w.

Tolerances: Topology and sample counts use exact integer operations. Wilson intervals and weighted counts agree with independent references within absolute error 1e-12. Finite samples need not share a common crossing or have value one half at p_e = 1/2.

Model limits

Static pure-erasure code capacity with known locations and perfect checks. Uncorrectable means that recovery cannot be guaranteed for every encoded state. It is not a sample of realized decoder failure.

No unknown-location Pauli decoder, measurement faults, mixed-loss threshold or threshold fit is included. Both logical sectors are necessary for this arbitrary-state criterion.

The exact one-half limit for the square toric family under pure erasure and optimal recovery comes from the percolation result discussed in the lesson. These finite samples do not prove that value.

The interactive supports L from 4 through 24 in steps of 4 and at most 1024 trials per size. Walk counting ends at length 10. Larger systems and longer walks are outside this display.

8.4 · Matching decoders

A single circuit fault often flips two detectors. Matching joins observed events into plausible fault paths, while allowing a path to end at a suitable boundary.

The detector construction assigns each fault its possible events. A detector graph places a vertex at every possible event location. An edge represents an independent fault variable with two endpoints, or one endpoint and an absorbing boundary. It also records whether that fault flips the logical observable. Begin with perfect-check ZZZ errors on the canonical rotated distance-three patch, so each edge is one data-qubit error.

The complete ZZZ-error graph follows from check incidence:

Data qubit Detector endpoints or absorbing boundary
1 aaa, left ZZZ boundary
2 a,ca,ca,c
3 ccc, right ZZZ boundary
4 aaa, left ZZZ boundary
5 a,ba,ba,b
6 bbb, right ZZZ boundary
7 ddd, left ZZZ boundary
8 b,db,db,d
9 bbb, right ZZZ boundary

The ZZZ boundary is named for its truncated ZZZ checks; a ZZZ string terminates there because the missing partner is an XXX check. The canonical labels and orientation are those of Module 4.

For independent edge variables ei∈{0,1}e_i\in\{0,1\}ei​∈{0,1} with probabilities 0<pi<1/20<p_i<1/20<pi​<1/2, likelihood becomes an additive cost:

−ln⁡P(e)=constant+∑ieiwi,wi=ln⁡1−pipi.-\ln P(e)=\text{constant}+\sum_i e_iw_i,\qquad w_i=\ln\frac{1-p_i}{p_i}.−lnP(e)=constant+i∑​ei​wi​,wi​=lnpi​1−pi​​.
(8.13)
Derivation · Factor out every no-fault probability

Keep the probability of absent faults while taking logarithms:

P(e)=∏ipiei(1−pi)1−ei=[∏i(1−pi)]∏i(pi1−pi)ei.P(e)=\prod_i p_i^{e_i}(1-p_i)^{1-e_i} =\left[\prod_i(1-p_i)\right]\prod_i\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)^{e_i}.P(e)=i∏​piei​​(1−pi​)1−ei​=[i∏​(1−pi​)]i∏​(1−pi​pi​​)ei​.

The first product is common to all candidate configurations. Its negative logarithm is the constant; each selected edge contributes ln⁡[(1−pi)/pi]\ln[(1-p_i)/p_i]ln[(1−pi​)/pi​]. More probable edges are cheaper. The approximation wi≈−ln⁡piw_i\approx-\ln p_iwi​≈−lnpi​ drops ln⁡(1−pi)\ln(1-p_i)ln(1−pi​) and is useful only for rare faults. The full log-odds rule follows from the independent graph model Sparse Blossom: correcting a million errors per core second with minimum-weight matching, PDF pp. 4–5 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.22331/q-2025-01-20-1600.

A matching pairs triggered events without using any event twice. Its pairing graph differs from the physical detector graph: the cost between two triggered vertices is the cheapest path through the physical graph. That path can pass through untriggered vertices. Boundaries can absorb several paths; treating an entire boundary as a single vertex that can be used only once would remove valid recoveries.

Join the two flags

Take pi=0.1p_i=0.1pi​=0.1 on every data edge and syndrome flags a,ca,ca,c. Each selected edge costs ln⁡(0.9/0.1)=ln⁡9=2.1972245773…\ln(0.9/0.1)=\ln9=2.1972245773\ldotsln(0.9/0.1)=ln9=2.1972245773…. The direct recovery Z2Z_2Z2​ costs 2.1972245773…2.1972245773\ldots2.1972245773…; Z1Z3Z_1Z_3Z1​Z3​ costs 4.3944491547…4.3944491547\ldots4.3944491547…. The direct chain is more likely under the independent model. The shared syndrome does not establish that Z2Z_2Z2​ actually occurred.

Compute an edge cost

For an independent edge fault with pi=0.1p_i=0.1pi​=0.1, what is its natural-log weight?

Explanation

wi=ln⁡[(1−pi)/pi]=ln⁡9=2.1972245773…w_i=\ln[(1-p_i)/p_i]=\ln9=2.1972245773\ldotswi​=ln[(1−pi​)/pi​]=ln9=2.1972245773…. The no-fault probability belongs in the numerator.

Finding the smallest total pairing cost requires revising earlier choices. Blossom algorithms grow alternating trees whose paths alternate between unmatched and matched edges. An augmenting path permits swapping those roles to match more events. An odd alternating cycle can obstruct the tree search; contracting that cycle into a temporary vertex lets the search continue. The algorithm later expands it consistently. This global revision is what a nearest-neighbor rule lacks Sparse Blossom: correcting a million errors per core second with minimum-weight matching, PDF pp. 7–8 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.22331/q-2025-01-20-1600.

Sparse Blossom carries out that search directly on the sparse detector graph. Its reported benchmark decodes both bases of a rotated distance-171717 surface code in under 1 μs1\,\mu\mathrm{s}1μs per round, for shots of 171717 rounds at circuit noise p=0.001p=0.001p=0.001. The model includes two-qubit CNOT depolarization, reset and measurement faults, and data depolarization before a round. The timing uses one Apple M1 Max core Sparse Blossom: correcting a million errors per core second with minimum-weight matching, PDF pp. 1, 24–25 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.22331/q-2025-01-20-1600. Hardware, noise density, and the amount of record processed all matter to such a comparison.

What is optimized?

What does minimum-total-log-odds matching select under its independent graph model?

Your answer

A union-find decoder trades minimum-weight optimization for cluster growth. A cluster is odd when it contains an odd number of flags. Odd clusters expand and merge until their flags can be paired internally or absorbed by a boundary. A spanning forest then keeps enough edges to connect each cluster without cycles. Peeling removes leaves one at a time, choosing an edge exactly when needed to cancel the leaf's flag Almost-linear time decoding algorithm for topological codes, PDF pp. 1, 3 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.22331/q-2021-12-02-595.

Peel a flagged path

Start with flags at v0,v3v_0,v_3v0​,v3​. The leaf v0v_0v0​ has only edge 010101, so select it and toggle flags at both endpoints. The flags become v1,v3v_1,v_3v1​,v3​. Remove v0v_0v0​ and repeat: choose 121212, leaving v2,v3v_2,v_3v2​,v3​, then choose 232323, leaving no flags. An unflagged leaf instead loses its edge without a correction. A tree's unique route makes these local decisions sufficient Linear-Time Maximum Likelihood Decoding of Surface Codes over the Quantum Erasure Channel, PDF pp. 2–3 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.2.033042.

For the bounded-degree toric-code problem, union-find has almost-linear complexity O(nα(n))O(n\alpha(n))O(nα(n)), where α\alphaα is the very slow-growing inverse Ackermann function. The weighted-growth variant reports thresholds near 9.9%9.9\%9.9% with perfect checks and 2.6%2.6\%2.6% with equal independent data and report noise Almost-linear time decoding algorithm for topological codes, PDF pp. 1, 7 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.22331/q-2021-12-02-595. The uniform growth sketch explains the mechanism; the performance numbers describe weighted growth. The perfect-check value sits below matching's roughly 10.3%10.3\%10.3% and optimal classes' roughly 10.9%10.9\%10.9% in the same one-type error setting.

Tangent: why nearest is not enough

Optional. Pairing the nearest events can discard the code's guaranteed correction ability.

Choose a starting flag uniformly, then a nearest partner uniformly among ties. A bad branch starts at 111 or 222, probability 1/21/21/2, and chooses the middle partner, probability 1/21/21/2. Its total probability is 1/41/41/4. Global minimum weight uses the two original edges and succeeds. The transfer exercise extends the count to the torus, following Browne's greedy-decoder problem Topological Codes and Computation, Problem Sheet 2: The Toric Code: Errors and Decoders, PDF pp. 3–5 Original source ↗. 8.5 · Degeneracy and maximum likelihood

Two equally short explanations can have unequal total support from longer errors. The decoder succeeds whenever it chooses the right logical class, so those extra explanations matter.

We now switch to an unrotated thirteen-data-qubit distance-three patch, with its own coordinate labels. The qubits are h(x,y)h(x,y)h(x,y) for x=0,1x=0,1x=0,1, y=1,2y=1,2y=1,2, and v(x,y)v(x,y)v(x,y) for x=0,1,2x=0,1,2x=0,1,2, y=0,1,2y=0,1,2y=0,1,2. A horizontal edge joins (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) to (x+1,y)(x+1,y)(x+1,y); a vertical edge joins (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) to (x,y+1)(x,y+1)(x,y+1). The six XXX stars, in order, are (0,1),(1,1),(2,1),(0,2),(1,2),(2,2)(0,1),(1,1),(2,1),(0,2),(1,2),(2,2)(0,1),(1,1),(2,1),(0,2),(1,2),(2,2). Endpoint stars outside these rows are absent.

Let A={v(0,0),v(1,1)}A=\{v(0,0),v(1,1)\}A={v(0,0),v(1,1)} and B={h(0,1),v(1,2)}B=\{h(0,1),v(1,2)\}B={h(0,1),v(1,2)}. Both trigger the first, second, and fifth stars. Their difference is a logical ZZZ times stabilizers, so they belong to different classes. Index horizontal edges first, row by row, then vertical edges row by row, assigning edge iii the bit value 2i2^i2i. For a definite minimum-weight tie rule, choose the smallest binary support integer. This selects AAA, with integer 272272272, ahead of BBB, with integer 204920492049.

Degeneracy here means that many different physical errors have the same syndrome and logical action. The weight enumerator Ah(w)A_h(w)Ah​(w) counts those errors of weight www in class hhh. It is unrelated to the overhead prefactor AAA introduced later. Its probability sum is

Wh(p)=∑w=0nAh(w)pw(1−p)n−w.W_h(p)=\sum_{w=0}^{n} A_h(w)p^w(1-p)^{n-w}.Wh​(p)=w=0∑n​Ah​(w)pw(1−p)n−w.
(8.14)
Derivation · Group the class sum by error weight

Start with Eq. (8.5) for independent ZZZ errors. Every weight-www pattern has the same probability pw(1−p)n−wp^w(1-p)^{n-w}pw(1−p)n−w. There are Ah(w)A_h(w)Ah​(w) such patterns in the class. Grouping equal-weight terms gives the displayed polynomial. All coefficients are nonnegative integers; their sum is the class size. This grouping keeps every stabilizer-equivalent explanation, including ones longer than the selected representative.

For this syndrome, each class has 646464 members. The complete coefficients are

The extra weight-three patterns favor BBB at small positive ppp. Not every coefficient favors it: AAA has more weight-four patterns. The full probability sum decides the winner.

The failure probability is its complement. The maximum is taken separately for each observed syndrome, so a good decision on one syndrome does not determine a whole-code threshold Efficient Algorithms for Maximum Likelihood Decoding in the Surface Code, PDF p. 3 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevA.90.032326.

Now return to Browne's torus from Module 3. Keep its original ten-error pattern, with coordinates measured from the upper left and yyy increasing downward. The shortest recovery has three edges. Their residual has eleven edges and vertical winding. Label classes relative to that recovery, so its class is 000000 and the drawn hidden error lies in 010101.

Confidence is not knowledge of the hidden path

Under independent ZZZ noise with perfect checks, the 000000 and 010101 posteriors are 0.9867020.9867020.986702 and 0.0132930.0132930.013293 at p=0.01p=0.01p=0.01. At p=0.05p=0.05p=0.05, they are 0.933220.933220.93322 and 0.066010.066010.06601. The remaining mass occupies classes 10,1110,1110,11. Both minimum weight and maximum likelihood select 000000 at these probabilities. Both fail on the drawn shot because it realizes 010101. The class comparison develops Browne's distinction between likely paths and likely classes Topological Codes and Computation: A lecture course given at the University of Innsbruck, May - June 2014 (full notes), PDF pp. 42–43 Original source ↗ Topological Codes and Computation, Problem Sheet 2: The Toric Code: Errors and Decoders, PDF pp. 1–2 Original source ↗.

Each board fixes one syndrome and compares its classes. p changes the independent ZZZ error prior from 0.0010.0010.001 to 0.50.50.5; show_counts reveals weight multiplicities. The bars show normalized class probabilities, the curve shows their variation with ppp, and the readouts show each decision's conditional risk. These are static, perfect-check calculations. The patch has open boundaries; Browne's board is periodic. A conditional comparison at one syndrome is not a threshold scan.

Can equal shortest paths lead to unequal classes?

On the thirteen-edge patch, both classes have one weight-two representative. What can the longer patterns change?

The classes contain the same number of stabilizer-related patterns, but those patterns have different weights. At p=0.1p=0.1p=0.1, BBB has the larger total probability. Counting only the shortest representatives loses that distinction.

Held fixed
  • Independent Z errors with probability ppp per data edge; perfect X-check outcomes (code capacity).
  • The unrotated distance-3 patch has 13 data qubits. Its six X checks are ordered (0,1), (1,1), (2,1), (0,2), (1,2), (2,2); the fixed syndrome is (1,1,0,0,1,0). Each logical class contains 64 errors.
  • A acts on v(0,0) and v(1,1), with packed edge mask 272. B acts on h(0,1) and v(1,2), with mask 2049. Horizontal edges are indexed row-major first, then vertical edges. Class A is relative to A; class B differs by a logical Z.
  • The minimum-weight rule minimizes the number of Z errors, then chooses the smallest unsigned edge mask. It chooses A on the small patch. At p = 1/2 this remains a geometric rule, although all individual errors are equally probable.
  • The Browne board is a 5 by 5 torus with 50 data edges. The fixed ten-edge error and three-edge recovery share flags at (2,1) and (3,4). Classes 00, 01, 10, 11 are relative to R, with horizontal winding first and vertical winding second. Each contains 16777216 errors.
  • The Browne coefficient tables include every weight from 0 to 50. The lowest weights are 3, 4, 6, 7, with 3, 4, 15, 35 representatives respectively.
Initial conditions
Static errors conditioned on a fixed syndrome; there is no random trial or time evolution. The default is the small patch at p = 0.1. Changing the board preserves p; a preset sets the values named in that preset.
Boundary conditions
The small patch has h(x,y) for x = 0,1 and y = 1,2, and v(x,y) for x = 0,1,2 and y = 0,1,2. X stars occupy the two interior vertex rows; Z plaquettes omit missing external edges. The top and bottom Z-boundaries absorb Z strings. Browne coordinates are periodic modulo 5 in both directions. In both drawings y increases downward.
Same flags, competing classes
A and B appear in separate panels with their shared flags. Browne shows E, R and E xor R separately, including the actual class 01 and recovery class 00. Select any check to inspect its data-edge support. Horizontal: zero-based lattice coordinates (n/a). Vertical: zero-based lattice coordinates (n/a).
Probability of each compatible class
Conditional probabilities of all two or four classes, normalized to sum to one. Small probabilities retain scientific notation. At p = 1/2 the probabilities are exactly 1/2 or 1/4. Horizontal: class (dimensionless). Vertical: conditional probability (dimensionless).
Decoder choices and conditional error
Minimum-weight and maximum-likelihood (ML) class choices, with conditional risk equal to one minus the chosen probability. A tie within 1e-12 selects the first class without changing the probabilities. Browne states whether each choice succeeds on the displayed error. Horizontal: Not applicable: textual readout (n/a). Vertical: Not applicable: textual readout (n/a).

Integer counts at weights 2 through 4 for the small patch or 3 through 7 for Browne. Show counts reveals all weights. Each column total is the size of its class. Horizontal: Not applicable (dimensionless). Vertical: Not applicable (dimensionless).
Class probabilities as p changes
Class probabilities at 201 evenly spaced probabilities from 0.001 through 0.5 plus the current p. The vertical cursor marks the current input. This fixed-syndrome curve does not estimate a code-family threshold. Horizontal: Z error probability p, .001.. .5 (dimensionless). Vertical: conditional class probability (dimensionless).

Method: Enumerate all 8192 Z-error supports on the small patch, retain syndrome 19, and classify by the parity of their difference from A on the logical X support. Count the errors at each weight. For Browne, use the four complete integer weight enumerators. Set t = p/(1-p), evaluate each polynomial by Horner’s rule and normalize; the common factor (1-p)^n cancels. Choose the largest class probability, using the first class on a tie within 1e-12. Subtract the chosen probability from one to obtain conditional risk. Reuse the same polynomial evaluation for the p sweep.

Tolerances: Class counts and support parities are integers. Probabilities agree with independent direct enumeration or face-spin transfer matrices within 1e-12 absolute error. The 1e-12 ML tie tolerance affects selection only; probabilities are never rounded before comparison or normalization.

Display conventions

  • Data qubits are rings; X checks are filled squares and Z checks are hollow squares. An e label and an outer ring mark a flagged X check. Z paths use dashes; class labels and dash patterns distinguish the curves.
  • Coordinates are zero-based and belong to the unrotated patch or the torus, separate from the rotated patch labels 1 through 9. Torus border copies identify the same checks and edges.
  • Probabilities use eight significant digits, risks six, and counts integers. At p = 1/2 the probability readouts show 1/2 or 1/4. Board panels stack vertically on narrow screens.

Model limits

Only these two fixed syndromes under independent Z-only code-capacity noise are included. Measurement and circuit faults, arbitrary syndrome selection and a code-family threshold are outside this model.

The small-patch disagreement depends on the declared minimum-weight tie rule. Other matching implementations can resolve that tie differently.

On the Browne presets, both decoders choose class 00 and fail on the displayed class 01 error. A maximum-likelihood class decision minimizes conditional risk; it need not identify a particular hidden error.

The board sizes remain fixed at 13 and 50 data edges. The browser enumerates only the small patch; the larger board uses its finite coefficient tables so parameter changes require only short polynomial sums.

Did optimal inference promise this shot would succeed?

Your answer

A tensor-network decoder organizes these sums using local probability factors connected by shared binary indices. Contracting the network means summing each shared index, so compatible local choices contribute to the class total. Intermediate arrays can grow large; truncation keeps the contraction manageable at the cost of approximation. For independent bit and phase flips with perfect checks, Bravyi, Suchara, and Vargo give a special O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) exact method. For general independent Pauli noise they instead give an approximate contraction controlled by its retained bond dimension Efficient Algorithms for Maximum Likelihood Decoding in the Surface Code, PDF p. 1 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevA.90.032326. The special tractable case does not cover arbitrary circuit histories.

You can now calculate why a class decision can beat a chain decision. Real devices also supply correlations that independent-edge models discard.

§

8.6 · Correlation-aware and learned decoders

A single fault can explain evidence in several checks at once. Treating those explanations separately throws away their shared cause. A stronger decoder can use that dependence.

The circuit noise model assigns probabilities to fault mechanisms, including mechanisms with more than two detector endpoints. Such a connection is a hyperedge. Separate XXX and ZZZ matching graphs discard some hyperedge information. For example, one YYY error contains both an XXX and a ZZZ component and can explain evidence in both graphs.

Write a Pauli, up to phase, as XxZzX^xZ^zXxZz. For depolarizing noise, P(I)=1−pP(I)=1-pP(I)=1−p and P(X)=P(Y)=P(Z)=p/3P(X)=P(Y)=P(Z)=p/3P(X)=P(Y)=P(Z)=p/3. The component probabilities obey

P(x=1)=P(z=1)=2p3,P(z=1∣x=1)=12(p>0).P(x=1)=P(z=1)=\frac{2p}{3},\qquad P(z=1\mid x=1)=\frac12\quad(p>0).P(x=1)=P(z=1)=32p​,P(z=1∣x=1)=21​(p>0).
(8.16)
Derivation · Condition on the shared Pauli cause

The possibilities with x=1x=1x=1 are XXX and YYY, each of probability p/3p/3p/3. Only YYY also has z=1z=1z=1, so

P(z=1∣x=1)=P(Y)P(X)+P(Y)=p/32p/3=12.P(z=1\mid x=1)=\frac{P(Y)}{P(X)+P(Y)}=\frac{p/3}{2p/3}=\frac12.P(z=1∣x=1)=P(X)+P(Y)P(Y)​=2p/3p/3​=21​.

The marginal P(z=1)=P(Z)+P(Y)=2p/3P(z=1)=P(Z)+P(Y)=2p/3P(z=1)=P(Z)+P(Y)=2p/3 can be much smaller. At p=0p=0p=0 the conditioning event has zero probability. The calculation isolates the shared cause: a detector event in a circuit usually supplies uncertain evidence for xxx, rather than revealing it with certainty.

Use the correlation

At total depolarizing probability p=0.03p=0.03p=0.03, suppose the XXX component is known to be present. What is the conditional probability that the ZZZ component is present?

It is 0.50.50.5. The remaining possibilities are equally likely XXX and YYY. Using the marginal 0.020.020.02 would ignore the new information.

Belief propagation exchanges probability messages on a factor graph. Variable nodes represent fault mechanisms; factor nodes enforce the observed detector parities. Each message summarizes what neighboring evidence says about one variable. The resulting marginal belief estimates how likely that fault is, conditional on the record.

Loops make these messages approximate. Independently choosing the most likely value of every variable can even violate a parity constraint. Belief matching uses the beliefs to reweight graph edges, then invokes matching to find a compatible explanation. This combines broader correlation information with an efficient compatibility solver Improved decoding of circuit noise and fragile boundaries of tailored surface codes, PDF pp. 2, 5 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevX.13.031007.

A neural decoder instead learns a map from measurement records to logical decisions. Bausch and colleagues use a recurrent state that carries information from earlier rounds. Attention lets one check's update depend on evidence from other checks. A readout predicts the logical correction. Training first uses simulated records, then fine-tunes on experimental records; held-out records test whether the learned rule generalizes Learning to Decode the Surface Code with a Recurrent, Transformer-Based Neural Network, PDF pp. 4–7 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08148-8. Training accuracy alone cannot supply that test.

8.7 · Real-time decoding

An answer can take many cycles to arrive while a pipeline still finishes one new answer every cycle. Those are different timing requirements. A useful decoder must handle both the incoming rate and the deadlines for using its answers.

Latency measures the delay from specified input availability to answer availability. Throughput measures how much input the system processes per unit time after its pipeline fills. A deadline concerns a particular answer; sustainable throughput concerns an ongoing stream.

For a simple queue model, measure arrivals and processing in the same work units. Let rgenr_{\rm gen}rgen​ be the constant arrival rate, rprocr_{\rm proc}rproc​ the constant processing rate, and Q0Q_0Q0​ the initial pending work. Treat work as divisible and let an empty queue idle:

Q(t)=max⁡{0,Q0+(rgen−rproc)t}.Q(t)=\max\{0,Q_0+(r_{\rm gen}-r_{\rm proc})t\}.Q(t)=max{0,Q0​+(rgen​−rproc​)t}.
(8.17)
Derivation · Integrate a constant rate mismatch

While work is waiting, its net rate is Q˙=rgen−rproc\dot Q=r_{\rm gen}-r_{\rm proc}Q˙​=rgen​−rproc​. Integrating from 000 to ttt gives Q(t)=Q0+(rgen−rproc)tQ(t)=Q_0+(r_{\rm gen}-r_{\rm proc})tQ(t)=Q0​+(rgen​−rproc​)t until the result reaches zero. A queue cannot be negative, so a faster server idles after emptying it. For constant rates this supplies the maximum with zero. In the serial example, arrivals are one item per time unit and capacity is one-half item per unit; with Q0=0Q_0=0Q0​=0, Q(t)=t/2Q(t)=t/2Q(t)=t/2 in this fluid approximation. A passive constant rate mismatch produces linear backlog growth.

A logical operation may need a decoded outcome before selecting its next control action. Define its reaction time, using consecutive nonoverlapping timing intervals, as

Treact=Tdecode+Tcontrol.T_{\rm react}=T_{\rm decode}+T_{\rm control}.Treact​=Tdecode​+Tcontrol​.
(8.18)Definition

Here TdecodeT_{\rm decode}Tdecode​ runs from the specified syndrome-input endpoint to the returned answer. TcontrolT_{\rm control}Tcontrol​ includes the remaining transfer and control delay until the chosen gate acts. A software-only latency should not silently stand in for the full reaction time Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold, PDF pp. 14–15 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y.

Google's real-time surface-code demonstration used a 727272-qubit processor at distance 555. Its cycle was 1.1 μs1.1\,\mu\mathrm{s}1.1μs. The reported 63±17 μs63\pm17\,\mu\mathrm{s}63±17μs latency ran from the decoding software receiving the final syndrome cycle to returning its correction, at the end of a shot. It remained roughly independent of shot length through 10610^6106 cycles. It did not include feedback into the logical circuit Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold, PDF p. 6 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y.

There is no contradiction between those times: many rounds are processed before the final input arrives. The sustained system kept up with the 1.1 μs1.1\,\mu\mathrm{s}1.1μs cycle. The offline neural decoder in that comparison required 24 μs24\,\mu\mathrm{s}24μs per cycle, a throughput figure Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold, PDF p. 6 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y. Accuracy and speed are separate measurements.

A sliding window processes a bounded span of recent rounds. Its older commit region contains corrections that become final. Its newer buffer supplies context for deciding whether apparent endpoints continue into later rounds. A correction crossing the cut leaves information for the next window to reconcile. Windows can run in parallel, but their overlap decisions must be made consistent Parallel window decoding enables scalable fault tolerant quantum computation, PDF pp. 2–5 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-42482-1.

Require it to exceed the incoming 1/τround1/\tau_{\rm round}1/τround​. The second expression assumes perfect load sharing and no reconciliation cost. A window budget

Suppose a worker finalizes ten rounds in 20 μs20\,\mu\mathrm{s}20μs. Its capacity is 10/20=0.510/20=0.510/20=0.5 rounds per microsecond. At 1.1 μs1.1\,\mu\mathrm{s}1.1μs per incoming round, the stream supplies 1/1.1=0.909090…1/1.1=0.909090\ldots1/1.1=0.909090… rounds per microsecond. One worker falls behind. Two ideal workers supply 111 round per microsecond and exceed the mean arrival rate. This arithmetic does not bound the slowest window or the cost of reconciling workers.

Why, then, do discussions of real-time decoding warn of exponential slowdown? The adaptive argument adds a causal loop. A non-Clifford gate can require a decoded result before the next layer is chosen. While the machine waits, error correction continues generating records. If decoding those new records takes even longer, each successive adaptive wait multiplies the work. For processing deficit f=rgen/rproc>1f=r_{\rm gen}/r_{\rm proc}>1f=rgen​/rproc​>1, Skoric et al. quote Terhal's lower bound proportional to fkf^kfk for an algorithm with kkk sequential adaptive TTT layers Parallel window decoding enables scalable fault tolerant quantum computation, PDF p. 1 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-42482-1. That argument concerns repeated feed-forward barriers; it is additional to the passive queue equation.

§

8.8 · From suppression to overhead

A suppression factor tells us how much one distance step helps. Turning that factor into a qubit count requires a curve to extrapolate, a target error rate, and a definition of which qubits count.

First return to measured rates, using a different dataset from the real-time experiment. Google's Fig. 1d compares distances 3,5,73,5,73,5,7 on its 105105105-qubit processor. Method: Evaluate the power law in logarithms. If the target is at or below a positive floor, no finite distance can attain it. Otherwise subtract the floor and divide by one minus the floor. Test distance 3 first. If it fails and the suppression factor is at most 1, no larger distance helps. In the improving regime, solve the logarithmic inequality, round upward to an odd integer, and check that distance and its predecessor. Use exact integer qubit arithmetic within the safe readout range. Independently repeat the solver after halving the physical probability. Plot odd distances through max(31, min(101, d+6)), or through 101 when no integer answer is displayed.

Tolerances: Distances and qubit counts are exact integers. Rate comparisons use relative-roundoff-aware logarithmic boundaries, never a fixed probability tolerance. Checks require relative rate agreement within 1e-10 above 1e-300 and exponent-conversion agreement within 1e-12.

Display conventions

  • Rates use scientific notation; the suppression factor and prefactor use six significant digits. Distance and qubit readouts are integers.
  • A solid line labels the baseline and a dashed line labels half noise. The vertical axis shows log10 of probability per QEC cycle; a value of -6 means one in a million.
  • Controls and readouts precede the full-width plot. All text fields accept scientific notation. Invalid entries show a field error and clear the numeric answer.
  • Convert A to preserve curve switches to the other exponent convention. If the converted prefactor would leave the control range, the action reports that limit without changing either input.

Commit your prediction above to start the lab, or skip it.

Model limits

This is a conditional forecast for a stationary code, noise model, and decoder. It does not infer a threshold from one physical gate metric.

A constant prefactor and continued power-law suppression are assumptions. If the suppression curve changes with distance, the forecast changes.

The floor represents an illustrative independent failure mechanism per cycle. Correlated failures need not obey this independent-event union model.

Counts include data and one measurement qubit per check. They exclude routing, spares, leakage-removal hardware, control hardware, logical gates, and factories.

At fixed prefactor, halving the baseline physical probability gives a suppression factor of 4.28. The separate improved-device forecast uses 4.5.

At most 50 odd distances per curve are plotted, keeping recomputation small. A finite solution may exceed the plot. When distance or total qubits exceeds Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, only logarithmic size estimates are displayed.

8.9 · Reconstruct and transfer

Rebuild the argument, then change its assumptions. The reconstruction and erasure transfer are core tasks; the rest are optional. State the code, noise model, decoder, and denominator whenever you compare numbers.

Rebuild the route from loops to classes

For independent ZZZ noise on an L×LL\times LL×L torus with perfect checks, reconstruct the minimum-weight decoder's sufficient low-noise bound. Derive the normalized face-spin class sum. What does matching optimize, and what does optimal recovery optimize?

Hint

Compare RRR with R⊕γR\oplus\gammaR⊕γ. Then count the possible roots and directions of a dangerous cycle. For the class sum, a selected face toggles its boundary and a global face-spin reversal changes nothing.

  • Proves the half-fault condition on a nontrivial residual cycle of length at least d=Ld=Ld=L.
  • Bounds its probability, counts placements, and sums a convergent sufficient bound.
  • Normalizes stabilizer-class sums with the correct Boltzmann sign and torus factor 1/21/21/2.
  • Distinguishes minimum energy from minimum class free energy on the Nishimori line.

Transfer the criterion to erased geometry

Classify the four erased supports. Why are size and seam contact insufficient? Peel v0−v1−v2−v3v_0-v_1-v_2-v_3v0​−v1​−v2​−v3​ with endpoint flags. What ambiguity remains if the support also contains a winding cycle?

Hint

Use both primal and dual graphs. At a tree leaf, only its incident edge can change the leaf's syndrome.

Check against the rubric
  • Classifies the seam edge and plaquette boundary as correctable and both winding supports as uncorrectable.
  • Tests the dual XXX cycle as well as the primal ZZZ cycle.
  • Chooses the three path edges in order and tracks the moving flag.
  • Distinguishes logical ambiguity from guaranteed failure on every shot.
Show model solution

The single seam edge is open. The plaquette cycle is a stabilizer. Neither supports a nontrivial logical. The horizontal row supports a primal ZZZ logical; the column of horizontal physical edges supports a dual XXX logical. The three four-edge sets therefore differ despite equal size.

Peeling selects 010101, then 121212, then 232323, moving the left flag until both cancel. With a winding cycle LLL, recoveries RRR and R⊕LR\oplus LR⊕L have equal syndrome but different logical actions. A spanning tree supplies a compatible representative, but cannot resolve this ambiguity. A guess can still succeed on one shot.

Transfer the greedy failure to a torus

Optional. On the five-cycle with errors 01,2301,2301,23, choose the first flag and a tied nearest partner uniformly. Prove failure probability 1/41/41/4. Hint

The bad first pair is the middle link 121212. The surviving flags then have a shorter connection through vertex 444.

Check against the rubric

Show model solution

Starting at 111 or 222 has probability 1/21/21/2. Choosing the other middle flag among its tied nearest neighbors has probability 1/21/21/2. The recovery is then 12⊕40⊕3412\oplus40\oplus3412⊕40⊕34; adding actual errors 01⊕2301\oplus2301⊕23 fills the cycle. The conditional failure probability is 1/41/41/4. Averaging the specified full-torus count gives

50122514=198=0.0102040816….\frac{50}{1225}\frac14=\frac1{98}=0.0102040816\ldots.122550​41​=981​=0.0102040816….

Any minimum-weight recovery has at most two edges because the actual two-edge error is a compatible candidate. Its residual therefore has at most four edges, fewer than distance five, so cannot be logical. The greedy recovery can have three edges and loses this guarantee.

Optional. In the odd m×mm\times mm×m Shor family, apply independent ZZZ faults with fixed 0<p<1/20<p<1/20<p<1/2 per qubit. With ideal checks, decode the row parities by majority. Find one row's odd-parity probability qmq_mqm​ and prove logical failure approaches 1/21/21/2 as m→∞m\to\inftym→∞. This extends Quantum Information, Chapter 7: Quantum Error Correction (Ph219/CS219 lecture notes, updated March 2026), PDF p. 87 Original source ↗.

Hint

The parity sign of one row has expectation (1−2p)m(1-2p)^m(1−2p)m. Couple its Bernoulli parity to a fair bit; the probability that any of mmm coupled bits differs is at most the sum of their biases.

Check against the rubric
  • Obtains qm=[1−(1−2p)m]/2q_m=[1-(1-2p)^m]/2qm​=[1−(1−2p)m]/2 from the parity-sign expectation.
  • Uses independent rows and bounds their joint distance from fair bits by m(1−2p)m/2m(1-2p)^m/2m(1−2p)m/2.
  • Concludes that majority failure approaches 1/21/21/2 for each fixed positive p<1/2p<1/2p<1/2.
  • Explains why growing minimum distance alone does not ensure a positive threshold for this family and decoder.
Show model solution

For each physical error bit eee, E[(−1)e]=1−2p\mathbb E[(-1)^e]=1-2pE[(−1)e]=1−2p. Independence within a row gives E[(−1)∑e]=(1−2p)m=1−2qm\mathbb E[(-1)^{\sum e}]=(1-2p)^m=1-2q_mE[(−1)∑e]=(1−2p)m=1−2qm​, hence the stated qmq_mqm​. Its bias from a fair bit is δm=(1−2p)m/2\delta_m=(1-2p)^m/2δm​=(1−2p)m/2.

Couple each row parity to a fair bit with mismatch probability δm\delta_mδm​. By a union bound, the probability that their entire vectors differ is at most mδmm\delta_mmδm​. Every event probability, including a majority, differs by at most that amount. An odd number of fair bits has a wrong-majority probability 1/21/21/2, by complement symmetry. Therefore

∣Pfail(m,p)−12∣≤m2(1−2p)m⟶0.\left|P_{\rm fail}(m,p)-\frac12\right| \leq\frac m2(1-2p)^m\longrightarrow0.​Pfail​(m,p)−21​​≤2m​(1−2p)m⟶0.

The exponential loss of each row's parity bias beats the increase in the number of rows. The limit holds for fixed positive ppp; it does not exchange the p→0p\to0p→0 and m→∞m\to\inftym→∞ limits.
